messages.text: The exact socket constructor now reaches the active `socket.socket` class record. Its class surface is partial, so I’ve added a narrow positive-member lookup: it accepts one complete direct method record only after the constructor-origin and stable-binding proof succeeds. The current focused run will confirm the method/signature join; unresolved or competing member records still stay incomplete.

The Paramiko workspace stand-in now passes. I’m tracing why the socket constructor’s exact origin is still lost before member dispatch, then I’ll finish the proof path, rerun the focused and regression gates, and commit the worktree changes.

The socket failure is narrower than the original dispatch gap: the flow solver sees three meetings from the same `socket.socket(...)` result, but declines to attach constructor-origin evidence. I’m checking the exact call-site source mapping and result IDs now; workspace class construction already proves the downstream receiver proof can close correctly.

The focused rebuild is still compiling the Python-enabled test target; the queue accepted it normally after I removed an overlong `TMPDIR` override that exceeded mbx’s Unix socket path limit. Once this run finishes, the call-site mapping will show whether constructor evidence can attach under the current one-call matching logic.

The call mapping is exact and uniquely identifies the constructor call and result value, so source association is not the cause. I’ve narrowed the remaining rejection to the meeting-level uniqueness guard; the next log will show which same-origin status or uncertainty predicate rejects the socket receiver while the Paramiko control still passes.

The flow now attaches the socket constructor call and result to the `.bind` receiver candidate. Its full policy proof still fails, so I’m instrumenting the independent binding/escape check; this will preserve the required guard against aliases, rebinding, and method replacement while locating the last rejected condition.

The receiver-origin candidate now survives the socket flow’s unproven-but-unambiguous path, and the Python adapter independently confirms one local definition, direct receiver use, and no alias or escape before closing the exact active-pack member. The next focused run checks both newly unpinned policies after removing diagnostics.

Both direct-dispatch policy fixtures now pass, including the external `socket.socket.bind` identity and the Paramiko workspace stand-in. I’m checking the remaining pinned dispatch probes next; only tests that complete and match their exact target will be unpinned.

The exact RQL dispatch route now passes for direct `TextIOWrapper.write`, and for both SMTP and FTP credential formals when each receiver is bound once. The original taint probe still needs a separate run because taint discovery also has to resolve the constructor calls themselves; that is outside this receiver-target proof.

Receiver-only policy tests now pass for socket, Paramiko, pathlib, SMTP/FTP, and TextIOWrapper. I’ve kept the taint tests pinned where their broader discovery still marks constructor/open calls unknown, and kept Pattern.search pinned because its compiled-pattern result has no direct-constructor proof. I’m reviewing the final diff and required lane checks now.

The receiver-origin route now proves exact dispatch for direct, stable instances of `socket.socket`, the Paramiko stand-in, `pathlib.Path`, `TextIOWrapper`, and SMTP/FTP methods. I’m checking the final diff and lane requirements, then I’ll run the regression gates, commit, and hand back the remaining pinned probes with their evidence.

The plan’s part 3 design now states the closure boundary and why no pack schema field is needed: exact, stable receiver evidence closes only the matching call; general `covers_overrides: false` behavior remains open. I’m now certifying the focused exact-identity probes before importing the current master tip and running the shared Python regressions.

The focused policy target is compiling under the lane’s cargo slot; it has not reported a test failure. Once it finishes, I’ll use that result to decide whether the remaining work is only broader regression validation or needs a code correction.

The direct SMTP/FTP identity probe is also compiling. The four dispatch proofs already passed; this separate check verifies that the newly selected method target still binds the exact `password`/`passwd` formal rows and excludes the short near miss.
`cargo fmt --check` found only formatting differences in the edited Python adapter and flow imports, so I’m applying rustfmt now. No semantic or test failure has surfaced.
Rustfmt is still traversing the workspace and has produced no errors. It’s a formatting-only pass; when it completes, I’ll check only the edited diff and continue with the regression run.

The delay came from `cargo fmt --all` invoking rustfmt over every crate and test target, rather than a build or hang. It is still progressing through that file set; I’m letting the formatting pass finish so it can apply the mechanical corrections consistently.

I added explicit policy near misses for a receiver alias, rebinding, and per-instance method replacement to the Paramiko stand-in fixture. That makes the RQL-level closure test exercise the same boundaries already covered in TypeFlow, and I’m rerunning it now.

The targeted rebuild is taking longer than the previous run because rustfmt touched the analysis crate and invalidated its artifact. It is still active under cargo-slot, so I’m letting the build finish before evaluating the new near misses.

The near-miss test is waiting in the MBX rustc wrapper: cargo-slot has started the build, but that wrapper has been idle for several minutes while other lanes are compiling too. The checkout and disk are healthy; I’m leaving the queued test alive and using the time to finish the review and report the exact remaining pins.

The cargo-slot compile advanced from the Python analysis crate to `brokk-bifrost-flow`, so it is making progress despite MBX latency. The plan now reflects the final call-local closure rule and keeps earlier part 2 validation as historical evidence.

The same build has moved through RQL, semantic packs, policy, runtime, and MCP crates; cargo is rebuilding the integration-test dependency graph, not reporting an error. After this check I’ll commit, fast-forward to the current master tip, and run the requested post-merge gates once.
The rebuild completed successfully after 10m53s, and the Paramiko RQL near-miss test is running now. The delay was compilation only; the five existing exact-dispatch checks have already passed.

The first RQL near-miss attempt exposed a distinction worth preserving: `resolved_call` can identify a workspace declaration even while dispatch coverage is open, and the policy run correctly becomes inconclusive. I’ve moved the negative checks to `call_bindings`, where the test can assert dispatch coverage directly instead of treating an open declaration candidate as a closed dispatch.

The new call-binding test hit a compile-time helper mismatch on its first build; I corrected it to use the workspace-aware query helper. I’m rerunning the two RQL checks now, and that compiler error is recorded in the evidence log.

This run is rebuilding the full dependency graph after rustfmt refreshed source timestamps across the workspace. It has not emitted a compile error; I’m letting the slot finish before deciding whether the new coverage assertions or implementation need adjustment.

The modified RQL and flow crates compiled successfully in the focused run; cargo is finishing downstream integration dependencies now. The direct-call test and the open-coverage near misses will determine whether the receiver assessment correctly overrides a statically exact but mutable instance dispatch.

Both RQL assertions pass: the direct stable instance is exhaustive, while alias, rebinding, and method replacement remain open. The initial exact-policy fixture also passes with only its reviewed positive calls, so I’m rerunning the complete set of six direct-instance probes against this implementation.

The first exact-dispatch batch passes 6/6. I added one further regression for an active stdlib-pack class: if a stable `TextIOWrapper` instance has its `write` method replaced, `call_bindings` must report open coverage. This directly checks the external-pack closure rule.

The seven focused direct-instance checks all pass, including the active-pack `TextIOWrapper.write` method-replacement case. I’m explicitly running the two remaining ignored probes now so the handback can distinguish actual dispatch gaps from ordinary suite skips.

The explicit Pattern probe still fails because `re.compile()` does not provide this direct-class constructor evidence. The socket sink fixture also remains incomplete for a separate taint-discovery reason, even after switching it to direct socket construction; the standalone exact `socket.socket.bind` dispatch policy passes. I’ve kept those two sink probes pinned with the new evidence.

The pre-merge Python semantic regression passes 107/107, including the constructor-origin TypeFlow cases. I’m finishing the pre-merge format and clippy gates, then I’ll merge the current master descendant and repeat the full requested regression set on the combined tree.
`cargo fmt --check` passes. Clippy is now checking the four touched packages with the Python feature enabled; it has compiled through the analysis crate and is still running without diagnostics.

Clippy found five routine issues in the new RQL code: a return binding, two `?` opportunities, an unnecessary option dereference, and an oversized parameter list. I fixed them by returning the expression directly, using `?`/`as_mut`, and grouping the TypeFlow request context in a small query struct; I’m rerunning clippy.

Clippy now passes on all four touched packages, and the full formatter check passes. I updated both remaining ignore reasons from the explicit probes: `re.compile()` lacks direct constructor evidence, while the separate socket taint sink is still incomplete in Python procedure discovery. I’m rerunning the focused exact-dispatch batch after the clippy cleanup.

The receiver-origin route is implemented, and the remaining work is to finish the focused run, merge current master, then run the required regression gates and commit the final tree. Two probes remain intentionally pinned where dispatch identity is proven separately but the broader taint policy still cannot close.

The focused direct-dispatch and negative receiver-origin tests pass. The current tree has only two dispatch-related pins left: `Pattern.search` lacks direct-constructor evidence, and the socket taint fixture still has incomplete procedure discovery. I’m preserving those while I move to the latest master and rerun the broader gates.

I merged current master into the lane commit cleanly. The post-merge Python semantic, cross-language, and analysis regression suites are running through `cargo-slot`; I’ll follow them with the dynamic-write/absent-member checks, the full Python policy suite, and clippy.

The analysis package is rebuilding after the merge; the other two checks are waiting on Cargo’s shared target lock, so there’s no conflicting build. Once that build finishes, the waiting test binaries can reuse the compiled artifacts.

The analysis build is still compiling the merged dependency graph, and the two waiting commands have not reported failures. I’m letting Cargo finish this single target build before starting the next gates.

The shared analysis compilation is CPU-bound rather than stuck; its `rustc` jobs are active. The two other `cargo-slot` requests remain queued behind the target lock, so I’m keeping the required checks intact and waiting for the build to release them.

The analysis get-type/get-definition filter passed 28/28. The semantic and cross-language commands are rebuilding the Python-enabled test binaries; their logs show compilation only so far, with no failures.

The merged analysis filter finished cleanly, and the remaining Python-enabled targets are now compiling their integration binaries. No test failure has appeared; the delay is the merged dependency rebuild.

The Python integration targets are still building, with active compiler processes and no test failures yet. The analysis-specific tests are done; after these two suites, subsequent checks should reuse the newly compiled artifacts.

Post-merge regressions passed: Python `suite_semantic` 107/107, structural Python search 11/11, and analysis get-type/get-definition 28/28. I’ve started the focused dispatch, dynamic-write, and Python absent-member filters next.

The focused dispatch probes passed 7/7, dynamic-write passed 17/17, and Python absent-member passed 9/9. I’m starting the full Python policy suite now; after it completes, only touched-crate clippy, formatting, and the plan/evidence update remain.
The full policy target is running 1,859 tests with its default nextest concurrency. It has passed the first 129 so far; some cross-language tests are slow, but no failures have appeared yet.

The full policy suite has passed roughly 580 of 1,859 tests. Two failures have surfaced so far: a Rust CQ07 sensitive-source completeness assertion and a Go latency classification test; both are outside the Python receiver-origin path and will be included with their log evidence.

The policy suite is past halfway at about 957/1,859. Three failures are visible so far, all in non-Python campaign or Go/Node baseline tests; I’m letting nextest report the full set before classifying them.

The policy run has reached about 1,254/1,859 and the PY17/PY10 Python model checks are passing. Nine failures are recorded so far, all unrelated Rust/Go/Node baseline cases; the run is continuing to catch any others.

The full run has reached roughly 1,391/1,859 with the same nine failures and no Python-model regressions. Several unrelated branch-relation tests have crossed the slow-test threshold, so completion may take a bit longer, but they are still running.
The full policy suite is at 1,717/1,859, still with nine failures. Python absent-member cases in the full run are passing; I’m waiting for the final tail and then will run clippy.

The full Python-feature policy suite completed: 1,850 passed, 9 failed, and 125 were skipped. All nine failures are in pre-existing Rust/Go/Node suite cases; I’ll include each name, concise cause, and the shared test log in the handback. The Python dispatch/model fixtures passed.

The full policy run finished with the expected nine non-Python failures and no new model-test failure. Clippy is rebuilding the merged analysis crate now; once it completes I’ll refresh the ExecPlan’s stale earlier counts and commit the final validation evidence.

I checked the Node buffer failure against the earlier passing run and found it is a regression from my RQL change: I recomputed dispatch for every language after model binding. I’m narrowing that update to receiver-proof cases, leaving non-Python dispatch untouched, then I’ll rerun that module and clippy.

Implemented #4411 part 3 and committed it at `bc07e6f686`, including the fix that restored the Node dispatch test. The Python regression filters and clippy pass; the full policy suite had 1,850 passes and 9 failures, detailed in [policy-suite-failures.md](/workspace/31e44e629cb2bbaa225a83cd820af443/bifrost/.worktrees/models-config/.agents/validation/issue-4411-part3/policy-suite-failures.md).

Integration is waiting on a parent decision: local master advanced to `3b6c115a14`, which reverts the TypeFlow prerequisite for part 3 after three `suite_semantic` regressions. I left that revert unmerged; the branch includes master through `53cc17b937`. The ExecPlan records the evidence and decision needed.

I submitted the handback report repeatedly. The tool accepted it but reports that Mjolnir has not picked up the request and may be stalled or restarting; it says the report may still be recorded.
